parent="1" style="text;html=1;whiteSpace=wrap;strokeColor=none;fillColor=none;align=center;verticalAlign=middle;rounded=0;" value="<b>Elastic IP<br></b>: static IPv4 address. Can associate with EC2 or network interface so that it's a fixed IP. When underlying EC2 fails, it can remap the address to another instance (e.g. Private IP of failed EC2 is not accessible, but the Elastic IP is available). Or for SSH, the IP always maintains the same even when you 'rebuild' the cluster<div>An elastic IP is accessed through IGW. If there is VPN set-up, it traverse through Virtual Private Gateway, not IGW</div>" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="30" width="270" x="-670" y="40" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="8ZnPT5LgEJRXauTFr2m2-100" parent="1" style="text;html=1;whiteSpace=wrap;strokeColor=none;fillColor=none;align=center;verticalAlign=middle;rounded=0;" value="<b>Elastic Network Interface (ENI)<br></b>virtual network card. Can attach to network interface, detach and reattach to another, so the network interface maintains the public and elastic IP addresses, private IP. Similar to assigning Elastic IP.<br>Usual purpose: create a management network, create dual-homed instances with workloads/ create low-budget, high availability solution.<br>But cannot assign to another EC2 in another AZ (defeats purpose of disaster recovery)" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="32.5" width="270" x="-660" y="230" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="8ZnPT5LgEJRXauTFr2m2-101" parent="1" style="text;html=1;whiteSpace=wrap;strokeColor=none;fillColor=none;align=center;verticalAlign=middle;rounded=0;" value="<b>Network Address Translation (NAT)</b><div><b>- </b>protect private IP addresses</div><div>- uses an Elastic IP as source IP address from private subnet</div><div>- different from IGW that NAT allow resources in private subnet to initiate outbound internet traffic (1 direction)<br><br>e.g. private IP 172.31.32.15 -&gt; goes through NAT becomes 172.31.2.15 (same as private IP in public subnet) -&gt; goes out of IGW to internet as 203.0.133.15 as the elastic IP style="text;html=1;whiteSpace=wrap;strokeColor=none;fillColor=none;align=center;verticalAlign=middle;rounded=0;" value="<b>When to use both?</b><div>Scenario: Web app in public subnet</div><div>SG: Inbound: HTTP (80) from 0.0.0.0 | Outbound: Allow all</div><div>NACL: Inbound: Allow 80 from internet | Outbound: Allow specific ports (1024-65535)</div><div>Why? Because responses go back through random ports<br><br>Use NACL when you want to block something globally, need explicit deny rules (backup firewall)</div><div>Always use SG by default</div>" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="30" width="477.5" x="1338.75" y="950" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> <mxCell id="8ZnPT5LgEJRXauTFr2m2-273" parent="1" style="shape=image;aspect=fixed;image=data:image/png,;" value="" vertex="1"> <mxGeometry height="408" width="423.78" x="1880" y="440" as="geometry" /> </mxCell> </root> </mxGraphModel> </diagram> </mxfile>

div.div:
Elastic IP
: static IPv4 address. Can associate with EC2 or network interface so that it's a fixed IP. When underlying EC2 fails, it can remap the address to another instance (e.g. Private IP of failed EC2 is not accessible, but the Elastic IP is available). Or for SSH, the IP always maintains the same even when you 'rebuild' the cluster
An elastic IP is accessed through IGW. If there is VPN set-up, it traverse through Virtual Private Gateway, not IGW

div.style: display: flex; align-items: unsafe center; justify-content: unsafe center; width: 268px; height: 1px; padding-top: 307px; margin-left: 11px;
box-sizing: border-box; font-size: 0; text-align: center; color: #000000;
display: inline-block; font-size: 12px; font-family: Helvetica; color: light-dark(#000000, #ffffff); line-height: 1.2; pointer-events: all; white-space: normal; word-wrap: normal;

div.div:
Elastic Network Interface (ENI)
virtual network card. Can attach to network interface, detach and reattach to another, so the network interface maintains the public and elastic IP addresses, private IP. Similar to assigning Elastic IP.
Usual purpose: create a management network, create dual-homed instances with workloads/ create low-budget, high availability solution.
But cannot assign to another EC2 in another AZ (defeats purpose of disaster recovery)

div.style: display: flex; align-items: unsafe center; justify-content: unsafe center; width: 268px; height: 1px; padding-top: 696px; margin-left: 11px;

div.div: - uses an Elastic IP as source IP address from private subnet

- different from IGW that NAT allow resources in private subnet to initiate outbound internet traffic (1 direction)
e.g. private IP 172.31.32.15 -> goes through NAT becomes 172.31.2.15 (same as private IP in public subnet) -> goes out of IGW to internet as 203.0.133.15 as the elastic IP address

div.div: - virtual firewall that controls both inbound and outbound traffic
- allows traffic based on IP protocol, port, IP address
- stateful rules (if inbound traffic is allowed, response is automatically allowed back like PING (user sends request -> server responds -> response is allowed)
- acts on network interface level e.g. EC2, RDS, ELB, not subnet level (unlike ACL), support ALLOW rules only
- Can chain SG -> internet to web app -> SG to link to app server -> SG to link to database

div.div: Scenario: Web app in public subnet
SG: Inbound: HTTP (80) from 0.0.0.0 | Outbound: Allow all
NACL: Inbound: Allow 80 from internet | Outbound: Allow specific ports (1024-65535)

Why? Because responses go back through random ports
Use NACL when you want to block something globally, need explicit deny rules (backup firewall)
